title: Coordination Compounds
description: Master Class 12 Coordination Compounds: Werner's theory, IUPAC nomenclature, isomerism, VBT and crystal field theory with solved examples and tests.

topics.title: Werner's Theory & Nomenclature
topics.concept:
A coordination compound contains a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or neutral molecules called ligands through coordinate (dative) bonds. Such compounds — e.g. [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 and K4[Fe(CN)6] — retain their identity in solution, unlike double salts (e.g. carnallite KCl·MgCl2·6H2O) which dissociate completely into their ions.

Werner's coordination theory (1893) explained these compounds with three postulates:

  • Every metal shows two kinds of valence. The primary valence is ionisable, satisfied by negative ions and equal to the oxidation state. The secondary valence is non-ionisable, satisfied by ligands and equal to the coordination number.
  • Primary valences are non-directional; secondary valences are directional and fix the geometry of the complex (e.g. coordination number 6 → octahedral, 4 → square planar or tetrahedral).
  • Ions in the secondary sphere (ligands) lie inside square brackets and are not precipitated easily; ions outside are free.

For [Co(NH3)6]Cl3, all three Cl− are primary (ionisable) and the six NH3 are secondary; adding AgNO3 precipitates all three chlorides. In [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 only two Cl− are ionisable.

Ligands are classified by the number of donor atoms (denticity): monodentate (one donor, e.g. Cl−, NH3, H2O, CN−); bidentate (two donors, e.g. ethane-1,2-diamine 'en', oxalate C2O42−); polydentate (e.g. EDTA4− is hexadentate). A polydentate ligand that forms a ring with the metal gives a chelate; such rings give extra stability (the chelate effect). An ambidentate ligand can attach through either of two donor atoms, e.g. NO2− (nitrito-N or nitrito-O) and SCN− (S- or N-bonded).

The coordination number (CN) is the number of donor atoms directly bonded to the metal (count donor atoms, not ligands). The coordination sphere is the metal plus ligands written inside the brackets and behaves as a single unit. The oxidation number of the metal is the charge it would carry if all ligand pairs were removed: for K4[Fe(CN)6], $x+6(-1)=-4\Rightarrow x=+2$.

IUPAC naming rules: (i) name the cation first, then the anion. (ii) Within the sphere, name ligands alphabetically before the metal. (iii) Anionic ligands end in -o (chlorido, cyanido, sulfato, hydroxido); neutral ligands keep their name except aqua (H2O), ammine (NH3), carbonyl (CO), nitrosyl (NO). (iv) Use di, tri, tetra for simple ligands and bis, tris, tetrakis for those whose own name has a multiplier (e.g. bis(ethane-1,2-diamine)). (v) The metal's oxidation state is a Roman numeral in parentheses. (vi) If the complex is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate (ferrate, cuprate, argentate, plumbate).

examples.solution:
1. Cation is the complex ion, named first; anion (chloride) last.
  2. Ligand: six NH3 = hexaammine.
  3. Oxidation state of Co: $x+6(0)+3(-1)=0\Rightarrow x=+3$.
  4. Metal is in a cation, so keep name cobalt with (III).

Answer: Hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride.

examples.problem: Name K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] and state the oxidation number and coordination number of iron.
examples.solution:
1. Cation potassium first; complex anion last.
  2. Six cyanido ligands = hexacyanido.
  3. Oxidation number: $x+6(-1)=-4\Rightarrow x=+2$.
  4. Anionic complex → metal becomes ferrate(II). CN = 6.

Answer: Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II); oxidation number $+2$, coordination number $6$.

examples.problem: Write the formula of the complex pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride.
examples.solution:
1. Co(III) with five NH3 (ammine) and one Cl− (chlorido) inside the sphere.
  2. Charge of complex ion: $+3+5(0)+(-1)=+2$.
  3. Balance with two outer Cl−.

Answer: [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2.

examples.problem: How many ions does 1 mol of [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Cl]Cl<sub>2</sub> give in water, and how many AgCl moles precipitate with excess AgNO<sub>3</sub>?
examples.solution:
1. Complex ion [Co(NH3)5Cl]2+ stays intact; two Cl− are ionisable.
  2. Total ions = 1 complex cation + 2 chloride = 3 ions.
  3. Only ionisable (outer-sphere) Cl− reacts with Ag+; coordinated Cl is not precipitated.

Answer: 3 ions per formula unit; 2 mol of AgCl precipitate.

1. Neutral complex; name as one word.
  2. Ligands alphabetical: ammine (a) before chlorido (c) → diamminedichlorido.
  3. Oxidation state of Pt: $x+2(0)+2(-1)=0\Rightarrow x=+2$.

Answer: Diamminedichloridoplatinum(II).

examples.problem: Identify the secondary valence (coordination number) and the primary valence of cobalt in [Co(en)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]Cl.
examples.solution:
1. en is bidentate: 2 en supply 4 donor atoms; 2 Cl inside supply 2 more → CN = 6 (secondary valence).
  2. Oxidation state: $x+2(0)+2(-1)=+1\Rightarrow x=+3$ (primary valence).

Answer: Secondary valence (coordination number) $= 6$; primary valence (oxidation state) $= +3$.

recap: A coordination compound has a central metal bonded to ligands by coordinate bonds; it keeps its identity in solution, unlike a double salt.
Werner: primary valence = ionisable = oxidation state; secondary valence = non-ionisable = coordination number; secondary valences are directional and fix geometry.
Ligands are mono-, bi- or polydentate; chelating ligands form rings (extra stability), and ambidentate ligands (NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>, SCN<sup>−</sup>) bind through either of two atoms.
Coordination number counts donor atoms (not ligands); oxidation number is found by balancing charges, e.g. K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] gives Fe as $+2$.
IUPAC: cation before anion; ligands alphabetical with -o for anions; metal oxidation state in Roman numerals; anionic complexes take the -ate suffix (ferrate, cuprate).

quiz.q: In [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Cl]Cl<sub>2</sub>, the number of chloride ions precipitated immediately by AgNO<sub>3</sub> is:
quiz.explanation: Only the two outer-sphere (ionisable) chlorides react; the coordinated Cl stays bound.

quiz.q: The coordination number of platinum in [Pt(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:
quiz.explanation: en is bidentate; two en give 4 donor nitrogen atoms, so CN = 4.
SCN<sup>−</sup> can bind through S (thiocyanato-S) or N (thiocyanato-N).

quiz.q: The oxidation state of nickel in [Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>] is:

topics.title: Isomerism & Bonding (VBT)
topics.concept:
Two compounds with the same molecular formula but a different arrangement of atoms are isomers. In coordination chemistry they fall into two families: structural (constitutional) isomerism, where bonds connect different atoms, and stereoisomerism, where the connectivity is the same but the spatial arrangement differs.

Structural isomerism includes:

  • Ionisation isomerism — the counter ion and a coordinated ligand swap places, giving different ions in solution, e.g. [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br and [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4.
  • Linkage isomerism — an ambidentate ligand binds through a different donor atom, e.g. [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]2+ (nitrito-N, yellow) vs [Co(NH3)5(ONO)]2+ (nitrito-O, red).
  • Coordination isomerism — ligands are interchanged between cationic and anionic complexes, e.g. [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6] and [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6].
  • Solvate (hydrate) isomerism — water is inside or outside the coordination sphere, e.g. [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 (violet), [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2·H2O and [Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl·2H2O (green).

Stereoisomerism includes geometrical (cis–trans) and optical isomerism. Geometrical isomerism appears in square planar [Ma2b2] (e.g. cis- and trans-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]) and in octahedral [Ma4b2] and [Ma3b3] (fac–mer) complexes. Tetrahedral complexes do not show cis–trans isomerism. Optical isomerism arises when a complex is non-superimposable on its mirror image (chiral), most commonly in octahedral chelates such as cis-[Co(en)2Cl2]+ and [Co(en)3]3+; the two forms are the dextro (d) and laevo (l) enantiomers.

Valence Bond Theory (VBT) treats bonding as overlap of empty hybrid orbitals of the metal ion with filled ligand orbitals (each ligand donates a lone pair). The hybridisation fixes the geometry:

  • $sp^3$ → tetrahedral (CN 4, e.g. [NiCl4]2−).
  • $dsp^2$ → square planar (CN 4, e.g. [Ni(CN)4]2−).
  • $d^2sp^3$ → octahedral using inner $(n-1)d$ orbitals (inner-orbital / low-spin, e.g. [Co(NH3)6]3+).
  • $sp^3d^2$ → octahedral using outer $nd$ orbitals (outer-orbital / high-spin, e.g. [CoF6]3−).

Whether a strong-field ligand pairs the d electrons (inner orbital) decides the number of unpaired electrons and hence the spin-only magnetic moment $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM. Limitations of VBT: it does not explain colour, gives no quantitative splitting energy, cannot predict the exact magnitude of magnetic moment, and offers no satisfactory reason why some ligands are strong-field and others weak-field.

examples.problem: Predict the hybridisation, geometry and number of unpaired electrons in [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> (NH<sub>3</sub> is a strong-field ligand).
examples.solution:
1. Co is +3 → $d^6$ ($3d^6$).
  2. NH3 is strong field, so the six d electrons pair into three $t_{2g}$-type inner orbitals; two empty $3d$ orbitals become available.
  3. Hybridisation uses inner d: $d^2sp^3$ → octahedral, inner-orbital (low-spin).
  4. All electrons paired → $n=0$.

Answer: $d^2sp^3$, octahedral, diamagnetic ($n=0$, $\mu=0$).

examples.problem: For [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (F<sup>−</sup> weak field), predict hybridisation and spin-only magnetic moment.
examples.solution:
1. Co is +3 → $d^6$.
  2. F− is weak field, so no pairing; configuration $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$ leaves the inner d filled.
  3. Outer $4d$ orbitals are used: $sp^3d^2$ → octahedral, outer-orbital (high-spin).
  4. Unpaired electrons $n=4$; $\mu=\sqrt{4(4+2)}=\sqrt{24}=4.90$ BM.

Answer: $sp^3d^2$, octahedral, $\mu\approx4.9$ BM (paramagnetic).

examples.problem: Why is [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> square planar and diamagnetic while [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is tetrahedral and paramagnetic?
examples.solution:
1. Ni is +2 → $d^8$ in both.
  2. CN− is strong field: it pairs the d electrons, freeing one $3d$ orbital → $dsp^2$ → square planar, all paired (diamagnetic).
  3. Cl− is weak field: no pairing; $sp^3$ → tetrahedral with 2 unpaired electrons (paramagnetic).

Answer: Strong-field CN− → $dsp^2$ square planar, diamagnetic; weak-field Cl− → $sp^3$ tetrahedral, $\mu=\sqrt{2(2+2)}=2.83$ BM.

examples.problem: How many geometrical isomers does the octahedral complex [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> show? Name them.
examples.solution:
1. Type [Ma4b2] octahedral.
  2. The two Cl can be adjacent (90°) or opposite (180°).

Answer: 2 geometrical isomers — cis (Cl adjacent) and trans (Cl opposite).

examples.problem: Identify the type of isomerism in the pair [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>(NO<sub>2</sub>)]Cl<sub>2</sub> and [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>(ONO)]Cl<sub>2</sub>.
examples.solution:
1. Same atoms; only the donor atom of the ambidentate NO2− changes (N-bonded vs O-bonded).
  2. This is a structural isomerism arising from the mode of attachment.

Answer: Linkage isomerism (nitrito-N vs nitrito-O).

1. The cis form has no plane of symmetry; the two chelating en rings make it chiral.
  2. Its mirror image is non-superimposable → two enantiomers (d and l).
  3. The trans form has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

Answer: Yes — cis-[Co(en)2Cl2]+ is chiral and exists as d and l optical isomers; the trans isomer is achiral.

recap: Structural isomerism: ionisation, linkage, coordination and solvate (hydrate) types — different atoms are bonded.

Stereoisomerism: geometrical (cis–trans; fac–mer in [Ma<sub>3</sub>b<sub>3</sub>]) and optical (chiral, non-superimposable d/l enantiomers, common in octahedral chelates); tetrahedral complexes show no cis–trans isomerism.
VBT: ligand lone pairs fill empty metal hybrid orbitals — $sp^3$ tetrahedral, $dsp^2$ square planar, $d^2sp^3$ inner-orbital octahedral, $sp^3d^2$ outer-orbital octahedral.
Strong-field ligands pair electrons (inner-orbital, low-spin); weak-field ligands do not (outer-orbital, high-spin); $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM gives the spin-only moment.
VBT limitations: it cannot explain colour, gives no $\Delta$ value, does not quantify magnetic moments, and does not explain the spectrochemical order of ligands.

quiz.explanation: The counter ion and a coordinated ligand have swapped, giving different ions in solution — ionisation isomerism.

quiz.q: The hybridisation of nickel in the square planar [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is:
quiz.explanation: Square planar geometry corresponds to $dsp^2$ hybridisation.

quiz.q: Which complex can show optical isomerism?
quiz.explanation: The cis-bis(en) octahedral complex is chiral (no symmetry plane) and exists as d/l enantiomers.

quiz.q: The spin-only magnetic moment of an outer-orbital $d^6$ octahedral complex (4 unpaired e<sup>−</sup>) is about:

topics.title: Crystal Field Theory & Applications
topics.concept:
Crystal Field Theory (CFT) treats the metal–ligand bond as purely electrostatic: ligands are point negative charges (or dipoles) that approach the metal ion and repel its d electrons. In the free ion the five d orbitals are degenerate, but the ligand field lifts this degeneracy — the orbitals pointing toward the ligands are raised, those pointing between them are lowered.

In an octahedral field, the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{z^2}$ orbitals (the $e_g$ set) point straight at the ligands and rise in energy, while $d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{zx}$ (the $t_{2g}$ set) point between ligands and fall. The energy gap is the crystal field splitting energy $\Delta_o$ (or $10\,Dq$). To keep the mean (barycentre) constant, $t_{2g}$ drops by $0.4\,\Delta_o$ and $e_g$ rises by $0.6\,\Delta_o$.

In a tetrahedral field the pattern inverts: the $e$ set ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) is lower and the $t_2$ set is higher, with a smaller gap $\Delta_t=\frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$. Because $\Delta_t$ is small, tetrahedral complexes are almost always high-spin.

The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by the field strength (size of $\Delta_o$ they produce): I− < Br− < Cl− < F− < OH− < H2O < NH3 < en < NO2− < CN− < CO. Weak-field ligands (small $\Delta_o$) favour high-spin complexes; strong-field ligands (large $\Delta_o > P$, the pairing energy) favour low-spin. For $d^4$–$d^7$ octahedral ions, electrons pair only when $\Delta_o > P$.

The net energy lowering relative to the unsplit case is the crystal field stabilisation energy (CFSE):

  • CFSE (octahedral) $= [-0.4\,n(t_{2g}) + 0.6\,n(e_g)]\,\Delta_o + mP$, where $m$ is the number of extra electron pairs formed.
  • For $d^6$ low-spin ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$): CFSE $= -0.4\times6\,\Delta_o = -2.4\,\Delta_o$ (plus pairing terms).

Colour: when $\Delta_o$ lies in the visible range, an electron is promoted from $t_{2g}$ to $e_g$ (a d–d transition); the complex absorbs that wavelength and shows the complementary colour. Larger $\Delta_o$ (stronger ligand) → higher absorbed energy → colour shifts toward violet. Ions with $d^0$ (Sc3+) or $d^{10}$ (Zn2+) are colourless — no d–d transition is possible. Magnetism follows the spin state: more unpaired electrons (high-spin) give a larger $\mu$. CFT therefore explains both colour and magnetic behaviour, which VBT could not.

Stability of a complex in solution is measured by the stability (formation) constant $K$: a large $K$ means the complex forms readily and dissociates little. Importance: coordination compounds are central to biology (haemoglobin contains Fe, chlorophyll Mg, vitamin B12 Co), to analysis (EDTA titrations for water hardness), to extraction of metals (gold/silver cyanide leaching), electroplating, and catalysis (e.g. Wilkinson's catalyst).

examples.problem: For [Ti(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> (Ti<sup>3+</sup> = $d^1$), write the $t_{2g}/e_g$ occupation and explain why it is coloured (violet).
examples.solution:
1. Ti3+ is $d^1$ → configuration $t_{2g}^1 e_g^0$.
  2. The single electron can be promoted $t_{2g}\rightarrow e_g$ by absorbing light of energy $\Delta_o$.
  3. It absorbs in the green–yellow region; the complementary colour transmitted is violet.

Answer: $t_{2g}^1 e_g^0$; a single d–d transition absorbs visible light, so the ion is violet.

examples.problem: Compute $\Delta_t$ if $\Delta_o = 18000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ for the same metal–ligand pair.
examples.solution:
1. Use $\Delta_t=\frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$.
  2. $\Delta_t=\frac{4}{9}\times18000$.
  3. $=8000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$.

Answer: $\Delta_t=8000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ (about 44 percent of $\Delta_o$, too small to force pairing).

examples.problem: Write the d-configuration of a $d^6$ ion in (a) a strong octahedral field and (b) a weak octahedral field, and give the number of unpaired electrons.
examples.solution:
1. Strong field ($\Delta_o > P$): electrons pair → $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$, $n=0$ (low-spin).
  2. Weak field ($\Delta_o < P$): maximum unpaired → $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$, $n=4$ (high-spin).

Answer: Strong field $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ ($n=0$); weak field $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$ ($n=4$).

examples.problem: Calculate the CFSE (in units of $\Delta_o$, ignoring pairing) for a high-spin octahedral $d^5$ ion.
examples.solution:
1. High-spin $d^5$: $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$.
  2. CFSE $= [-0.4\times3 + 0.6\times2]\,\Delta_o$.
  3. $= [-1.2 + 1.2]\,\Delta_o = 0$.

Answer: CFSE $= 0$ (a half-filled high-spin $d^5$ has zero crystal field stabilisation).

examples.problem: Arrange [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup>, [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> and [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> in increasing order of $\Delta_o$.
examples.solution:
1. Same metal ion (Co3+); $\Delta_o$ depends on ligand field strength.
  2. From the spectrochemical series: F− < H2O < NH3.

Answer: [CoF6]3− < [Co(H2O)6]3+ < [Co(NH3)6]3+.

examples.problem: Why is [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> deep blue while [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is pale blue?
examples.solution:
1. NH3 is a stronger field ligand than H2O, so it gives a larger $\Delta_o$.
  2. Larger $\Delta_o$ → light of higher energy (shorter wavelength) absorbed, shifting absorption and so the observed colour deepens.
  3. Hence the ammine complex is a far more intense (deep) blue.

Answer: Stronger-field NH3 increases $\Delta_o$, shifting the d–d absorption and intensifying the colour to deep blue.

recap: CFT is electrostatic: ligand point charges split the degenerate d orbitals — octahedral gives lower $t_{2g}$ and higher $e_g$ separated by $\Delta_o$ ($t_{2g}$ down $0.4\,\Delta_o$, $e_g$ up $0.6\,\Delta_o$).
Tetrahedral splitting is inverted and smaller: $\Delta_t=\frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$, so tetrahedral complexes are almost always high-spin.

Spectrochemical series I<sup>−</sup> < Br<sup>−</sup> < Cl<sup>−</sup> < F<sup>−</sup> < H<sub>2</sub>O < NH<sub>3</sub> < en < CN<sup>−</sup> < CO; strong field ($\Delta_o > P$) gives low-spin, weak field gives high-spin.
Colour arises from d–d transitions ($t_{2g}\rightarrow e_g$); $d^0$ and $d^{10}$ ions are colourless; larger $\Delta_o$ shifts the colour toward violet.

CFSE measures the stabilisation; stability constants $K$ measure how strongly a complex forms; coordination compounds are vital in biology (haemoglobin, chlorophyll, B<sub>12</sub>), analysis (EDTA), metallurgy and catalysis.

quiz.q: In an octahedral field the orbitals raised in energy ($e_g$ set) are:
quiz.explanation: The $e_g$ orbitals $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{z^2}$ point at the ligands and are raised.

quiz.q: The relationship between tetrahedral and octahedral splitting is:
quiz.explanation: For the same metal and ligands, $\Delta_t=\frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$, which is why tetrahedral complexes are high-spin.
A $d^{10}$ ion has no empty d level for a d–d transition, so it is colourless.

quiz.q: A strong-field ligand produces a low-spin complex when:
quiz.explanation: Pairing occurs (low-spin) only when the splitting exceeds the pairing energy, $\Delta_o > P$.

questions.q: A coordination compound differs from a double salt because it:
options: Retains its complex ion in solution
questions.explanation: The complex ion of a coordination compound stays intact in solution; a double salt dissociates fully.

questions.q: The primary valence in Werner’s theory equals the:

questions.q: The coordination number of Co in [Co(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is:

questions.q: The IUPAC name of K<sub>3</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] is:
questions.explanation: Fe is +3 ($x-6=-3$); anionic complex → ferrate(III).

questions.q: Which is an ambidentate ligand?
questions.explanation: NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> binds through N (nitrito-N) or O (nitrito-O).

questions.q: EDTA<sup>4−</sup> acts as a ligand of denticity:
questions.explanation: EDTA<sup>4−</sup> has six donor atoms (2 N + 4 O), hexadentate.

questions.q: The pair [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub> and [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]Cl<sub>2</sub>·H<sub>2</sub>O are:
questions.explanation: Water moves between inside and outside the coordination sphere — solvate isomerism.

questions.q: Square planar geometry corresponds to the hybridisation:
questions.explanation: Square planar four-coordinate complexes use $dsp^2$.

questions.q: An inner-orbital octahedral complex has hybridisation:
questions.explanation: Inner-orbital (low-spin) octahedral complexes use inner $(n-1)d$: $d^2sp^3$.

questions.explanation: Weak-field Cl<sup>−</sup> → $sp^3$ tetrahedral, $d^8$ with 2 unpaired e<sup>−</sup>.

questions.q: The spin-only moment of [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> ($d^6$, high-spin) is about:
questions.explanation: 4 unpaired electrons: $\mu=\sqrt{4(4+2)}=4.90$ BM.

questions.q: Which complex can show optical isomerism?
questions.explanation: cis-bis(en) is chiral (no symmetry plane) — d/l enantiomers.

questions.q: In an octahedral field the lower-energy set of d orbitals is:
questions.explanation: $t_{2g}$ points between ligands and is stabilised by $0.4\,\Delta_o$.

questions.q: The value of $\Delta_t$ relative to $\Delta_o$ is:
questions.explanation: $\Delta_t=\frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ for the same metal and ligands.

questions.q: A low-spin octahedral complex forms when:
questions.explanation: Pairing (low-spin) needs the splitting to exceed the pairing energy.

questions.q: Which ion is colourless?
questions.explanation: Sc<sup>3+</sup> is $d^0$; no d–d transition is possible.

questions.q: The metal present in vitamin B<sub>12</sub> is:
questions.explanation: Vitamin B<sub>12</sub> (cyanocobalamin) contains cobalt.

questions.q: The CFSE of a low-spin octahedral $d^6$ ion (ignoring pairing terms) is:
questions.explanation: $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$: CFSE $=6\times(-0.4)\,\Delta_o=-2.4\,\Delta_o$.

questions.q: A 3d $M^{3+}$ complex is octahedral, low-spin and diamagnetic. If $M^{3+}$ is $d^6$, the number of unpaired electrons is:
questions.explanation: Low-spin $d^6$ = $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$, so 0 unpaired electrons (diamagnetic).

questions.q: If $\mu = 5.92$ BM for a complex, the number of unpaired electrons is:
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{n(n+2)}=5.92\Rightarrow n=5$.

questions.q: For [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> (Cr<sup>3+</sup> = $d^3$), the spin-only moment is:
questions.explanation: $d^3$ has 3 unpaired e<sup>−</sup>: $\mu=\sqrt{3(3+2)}=3.87$ BM.

questions.q: The total number of ions produced in solution by 1 formula unit of [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub> is:
questions.explanation: One complex cation + three Cl<sup>−</sup> = 4 ions.

questions.q: How many geometrical isomers exist for octahedral [Ma<sub>3</sub>b<sub>3</sub>]?
questions.explanation: The fac and mer arrangements give 2 geometrical isomers.

questions.q: Among [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> ($d^5$ low-spin) the number of unpaired electrons is:
questions.explanation: Low-spin $d^5$ = $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$, so 1 unpaired electron.

questions.q: Which arrangement of $\Delta_o$ (increasing) is correct for Co<sup>3+</sup>?
questions.explanation: Spectrochemical order: F<sup>−</sup> < H<sub>2</sub>O < CN<sup>−</sup>.

questions.q: The number of unpaired electrons in tetrahedral [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> ($d^8$) is:
questions.explanation: High-spin tetrahedral $d^8$ ($e^4 t_2^4$) has 2 unpaired electrons.

questions.q: For the octahedral series, which $d^n$ high-spin ion has CFSE = 0?
The hybridisation and unpaired electrons of [Mn(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (Mn<sup>3+</sup>=$d^4$, strong field) are:
questions.explanation: Strong-field CN<sup>−</sup>: low-spin $t_{2g}^4$ → $d^2sp^3$, 2 unpaired electrons.

questions.q: One mole of [Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>4</sub> gives how many ions in water?
questions.explanation: One complex cation + four Cl<sup>−</sup> = 5 ions.
